title: Client Communication
description: Scenario-based practice for the conversations that decide whether a client stays: unclear briefs, urgent messages, managing expectations and knowing when to escalate.
objectives: Respond to requests with clarity and a next step
Turn an unclear brief into a usable one without friction
Recognise when to escalate — and to whom

cards.title: Clients do not buy campaigns. They buy confidence.
cards.body: Every message you send either adds to that confidence or takes from it.

cards.title: Reply within the hour, even without the answer
cards.body: “Got it, looking into this now, I will update you by 3pm” is a complete reply. Silence is not.

cards.title: Headline first, reasons second
cards.body: Say what you recommend, then why. Clients skim; make the first sentence the one that matters.

cards.title: Never blame the platform, the data or the intern
cards.body: Clients forgive mistakes. They do not forgive excuses.

expandable.label: An example
expandable.body: “The conversion tracking was misconfigured on our side; we fixed it this morning and here is the corrected number.” That sentence costs nothing and buys trust.

cards.title: A problem you share is half the size
cards.body: If you cannot fix it today, your account director needs to know today. Escalation is not failure; late escalation is.

check.question: When should you escalate a problem you cannot fix yourself?

modules.title: The unclear brief
modules.instructions: A client sends: “We want to do something on TikTok, maybe next month, budget TBD. Thoughts?”

options.text: “Great idea! We will put a plan together.”
options.explanation: Enthusiastic, but you still know nothing. The plan will be a guess.

options.text: “Happy to. To scope it, could you share the goal, the audience and a rough budget range? A 20-minute call this week would cover it.”
options.explanation: Positive, specific, and it proposes the next step.

options.text: “We need a proper brief before we can look at this.”
options.explanation: Correct in substance, cold in tone.

questions.prompt: The client replies: “Budget is whatever gets results.” Select every good next move.

options.text: Offer two or three budget scenarios with expected outcomes
Ask what result would make the pilot a success
Start building with a budget you think is reasonable
options.explanation: Never spend money that was not explicitly approved.

options.text: Explain that TikTok needs a minimum test budget to learn anything

questions.explanation: Vague budgets become concrete when you attach outcomes to numbers.

modules.title: The unhappy client
modules.instructions: Harbor Supply Co. is three weeks into a paid-social campaign and the numbers are not where they hoped. Every choice shapes how this ends.

content.intro:
It is Tuesday, 9:40. Your account lead forwards a two-line email from **Dana Whitfield**, Head of Growth at Harbor Supply Co.: *"Can we talk today? Campaign results are not what we signed up for."*

The campaign has spent **$18,400** of a $30,000 budget. CPA is **$62** against a $45 target. You have 20 minutes before the call.

nodes.speaker: Dana, Head of Growth
nodes.title: The call opens cold
nodes.text:
"I'll be direct. We're over 60% through the budget and CPA is almost 40% above target. My CFO is asking why we're still spending. What's going on?"

You have the dashboard open. Conversion rate from the landing page dropped from 3.1% to 1.9% after their site team redesigned the checkout two weeks ago. Ad CTR is actually up.

choices.text: Acknowledge the gap, then ask what the CFO needs to see by Friday.
choices.feedback: You validated the concern without defending yet, and you found out what a good outcome looks like for *her*. That gives you a target.

choices.text: Explain that the checkout redesign on their side is what tanked conversion.
choices.feedback: You may be right, but leading with blame on a tense call makes the client defend her own team instead of listening to you.

choices.text: Offer to pause spend immediately while you investigate.
choices.feedback: Safe, and it shows you take the budget seriously. But pausing without a diagnosis loses momentum and learning data.

nodes.speaker: Dana, Head of Growth
nodes.title: A door opens
nodes.text:
"Honestly? He needs to see CPA trending toward $45 and a plan with dates. I don't need a miracle, I need to not look blindsided."

You now share your screen: CTR is up 22%, but landing-page conversion halved the day the new checkout went live. The cause is almost certainly on their site, not in the ads.

choices.text: Walk through the data together and propose a joint fix: a two-step checkout test on their side, retargeting shifted to cart abandoners on yours.
choices.feedback: You framed the finding as a shared problem with a shared fix. Dana now has something concrete to bring to her CFO, and it includes her team.

choices.text: Show the conversion drop and suggest their site team should look into it before you change anything.
choices.feedback: Accurate, but it hands the problem back over the fence. Dana hears "not our fault" even if you did not say it.

choices.text: Promise to cut CPA to $45 by Friday by reallocating all spend to the best-performing audience.
choices.feedback: You cannot fix a landing-page problem with media allocation. Overpromising to end an uncomfortable call sets up a worse one next week.

nodes.speaker: Dana, Head of Growth
nodes.title: Walls go up
nodes.text:
"So this is our fault? The checkout was redesigned because *your* team said the old one was slow on mobile. I'm not going to the CFO with 'the agency says it's us.'"

The call has turned into a negotiation about blame. You can still turn it around, but it will cost something.

choices.text: Back up: "You're right, that came out wrong. Let's look at the numbers together and figure out what we can each fix this week."
choices.feedback: A clean reset. Owning the misstep quickly costs you less than digging in. Dana is willing to look at the data now.

choices.text: Hold your ground and send the analytics export after the call as proof.
choices.feedback: Being right and being retained are different things. Proof delivered after a hostile call reads as a paper trail, not a partnership.

nodes.speaker: Dana, Head of Growth
nodes.title: Spend paused
nodes.text:
"Okay. Pause it. But I need to know by Thursday whether this campaign is salvageable or whether we're writing off the quarter."

With spend paused you have 48 hours and no new data. The conversion drop on their checkout is still the real story.

choices.text: Use the pause to run a quick checkout audit with their dev lead and come back Thursday with a joint plan.
choices.feedback: You turned a pause into a diagnostic window and brought their team in. Thursday's meeting now has a story and a plan.

choices.text: Rebuild the ad creative and audiences from scratch so you have something new to show on Thursday.
choices.feedback: New creative does not fix a checkout that lost half its conversions. You will show effort on Thursday, not a solution.

nodes.title: Renewed, with a plan
nodes.text:
Thursday's follow-up has Dana, her dev lead, and you on the same slide: CTR up 22%, checkout fix shipping Monday, retargeting live on cart abandoners. CPA drops to **$48** within ten days.

Dana's CFO signs off on the remaining budget. Three weeks later she asks about Q3.
nodes.summary: The winning pattern: acknowledge first, diagnose together, propose a fix that includes the client's team. Being right about the cause mattered less than how you shared it.

nodes.title: Still on the account, barely
nodes.text:
Their site team eventually fixes the checkout, but it takes three weeks and nobody at Harbor connects the recovery to you. The campaign finishes at a **$55 CPA**.

Dana keeps the contract through the quarter and opens an RFP for next year.
nodes.summary: You were accurate but passive. Handing a problem back over the fence protects you in the moment and costs you the relationship over time. Clients remember who helped, not who was right.

nodes.title: The Friday call
nodes.text:
Friday arrives. CPA is **$59**. Reallocating spend did nothing because the leak was on the landing page, and now Dana has told her CFO a number you cannot deliver.

"I defended you on Tuesday. I'm not doing that twice." The account moves to a 30-day notice.
nodes.summary: Promises made to end an uncomfortable conversation turn into a worse conversation later. Diagnose before you commit, and never commit to a fix outside your control.

nodes.title: Churned
nodes.text:
Your analytics export is correct and nobody reads it. Dana forwards the thread to procurement with one line: *"Not a fit."*

The campaign ends at **$64 CPA** with $9,000 unspent. Harbor Supply Co. signs with another agency in June.
nodes.summary: A tense client call is not a court case. Winning the argument about whose fault it was cost you the account. Lead with the relationship, then bring the data.

feedback.complete: Try another path to see how the same facts land differently depending on how you lead the conversation.

modules.title: Urgent client message on Friday 5pm
modules.instructions: Priya runs marketing at Harbor Supply Co. It is 5:02pm on a Friday and she has just messaged you. Pick the reply you would actually send.

messages.text: The spring sale ads are showing the **old 15% code** instead of the 25% one. Our support inbox is filling up and the sale went live an hour ago.

responses.text: I'm here. Pausing the affected ads now and I'll confirm in 5 minutes which placements had the old code.
responses.feedback: You answered the question she did not ask: *is anyone handling this?* Concrete action plus a time box lowers her stress immediately.

responses.text: That's odd, the brief we got had 15% in it. Can you double check what was sent over?
responses.feedback: Even if the brief was wrong, 5pm on a Friday with a live sale is not the moment. She hears *not our problem* while customers are seeing the wrong code.

responses.text: Oh no, sorry to hear that! Let me look into it and get back to you.
responses.feedback: Warm but empty. *Get back to you* when? Doing what? With a live problem, the client needs a specific next action.

messages.text: Okay, thank you. I can see spend has stopped.
It was three of the five ad sets, right? Those are the ones people are complaining about.

responses.text: Correct, three ad sets. The fix is a creative swap, about 20 minutes to rebuild and resubmit. I'd rather push the right version tonight than leave the sale dark over the weekend. Okay with you?
responses.feedback: You confirmed the scope, gave an estimate, and offered a recommendation with a reason. Asking for her go-ahead keeps her in control.

responses.text: Yes. I'll fix it Monday first thing so we don't rush changes at this hour.
responses.feedback: Caution is reasonable, but a sale is running *now*. Leaving it paused all weekend turns a 20-minute fix into a lost weekend of revenue.

messages.text: Live again with 25%. Just placed a test order myself, code works.
Honestly I was dreading this message. Thanks for jumping on it.

responses.text: Glad it's sorted. I'll send a short note Monday on how the old code slipped through and what we're changing so it doesn't happen again. Enjoy your weekend.
responses.feedback: You closed the loop *and* pre-empted the post-mortem question before she had to ask it. This is how trust is built after a mistake.

responses.text: No problem at all! Have a great weekend.
responses.feedback: Perfectly pleasant, but it leaves the *why did this happen* conversation for Monday, when she may already be asking it.

messages.text: Sale is our biggest weekend of the quarter and ads are off. Can we really not get this live today?

responses.text: You're right, I should have offered that last night. Rebuilding the three ad sets now, live within the hour.
responses.feedback: A quick, specific recovery. You lost some goodwill overnight, but owning it without excuses gets most of it back.

responses.text: I can't make changes to live campaigns on weekends without a change request from your side.
responses.feedback: Process is there to protect the client, not to stop you from helping them. Quoting it during their biggest weekend reads as hiding.

messages.text: I'm not trying to assign blame, I'm trying to stop customers from seeing the wrong discount.
Can you pause them or not?

responses.text: Yes, sorry, pausing the affected ad sets now. I'll confirm in 5 minutes and we can sort out the brief on Monday.
responses.feedback: Good recovery. You dropped the argument and moved to action. Parking the brief question for Monday is the right call.

responses.text: I can, but I want to be clear this wasn't an error on our side.
responses.feedback: Twice defensive. She now has a live problem *and* an agency that seems more worried about fault than fixing it.

messages.text: Any update? Support says 40 tickets now.

responses.text: Yes. Three of five ad sets had the old code. They're paused as of now and I can have the corrected version live in about 20 minutes if you want me to push it tonight.
responses.feedback: Specific, scoped and actionable. Twenty minutes late, but this is the message she needed from the start.

responses.text: Still digging into it, will let you know as soon as I have something.
responses.feedback: Forty tickets and no action. Vague updates during an incident are worse than silence because they confirm nothing is happening.

messages.text: That would be great. Really appreciate it. Have a good one.

nodes.summary: You treated an awkward Friday message as a chance to show how the agency behaves under pressure: act first, scope the problem, recommend with a reason, close the loop. Priya will remember the recovery more than the mistake.

The problem got fixed and the relationship is intact, but there was room to be faster or more explicit about what happens next. Notice where a specific commitment would have saved a follow-up message.

messages.text: Hi. Can we set up a call with your account director this week? We need to talk about how incidents get handled.

nodes.summary: Priya did not need an explanation, a brief review, or a process reminder. She needed the wrong discount to stop appearing. When a client is in a live problem, lead with action and keep accountability conversations for later.

modules.title: Monday, 9:00 — your inbox at Brightline Media
modules.instructions: You're Jordan, an account manager at Brightline Media. The all-hands starts at 10:00 and seven messages are waiting. Open each one and decide what to do with it. Names and figures are fictional.

actions.label: Reply now
actions.description: Needs you personally, before anything else.

actions.label: Delegate
actions.description: Someone else owns it. Hand it over with context.

actions.label: Schedule
actions.description: Important, not urgent. Book time for it.

actions.label: Archive
actions.description: Nothing to do. Clear it out.

actions.label: Report
actions.description: Looks like a scam. Send it to IT security.

messages.subject: Conversions at zero since midnight?
messages.preview: The shared Pulse dashboard shows zero purchases from paid social since 00:00, but orders are still coming in…
messages.body:
Hi Jordan,

The Pulse dashboard you share with us shows **zero** conversions from paid social since midnight, but our store is still taking orders, so people are clearly buying. Either tracking broke or the ads stopped working.

Our CEO reviews this dashboard at 10:00 every Monday. Can you tell me what's going on before then?

Priya
messages.explanation: **Reply now.** A VIP client, a live problem and a deadline about an hour away: this is the one message that cannot wait. Acknowledge it within minutes, say what you are checking (orders on the site but zero tracked conversions points to a broken tag, not dead ads) and promise an update before her 10:00. Pull in Analytics *after* you have replied; delegating without a word leaves her alone with the problem.

messages.subject: Action required: your ad account will be suspended in 24 hours
messages.preview: We detected unusual activity. Verify your password within 24 hours to keep your campaigns running…
messages.body:
Dear Advertiser,

We detected unusual sign-in activity on your **Adwave Ads** account. To avoid suspension of all active campaigns, verify your password within 24 hours:

`adwave-busines.com/verify-account`

If you do not verify, your campaigns will stop serving and any outstanding balance will be charged immediately.

Adwave Business Support
messages.explanation: **Report.** Look past the panic: a generic greeting, a 24-hour threat, a request for your password and a sender domain one letter off (`adwave-busines.com`). Real ad platforms never ask for a password by email. Don't click, don't reply and don't forward it around as a warning: report it so IT security can block the domain for everyone. If you're worried, sign in through the bookmark you always use.

messages.subject: Approval needed: Northwind spring banners (live at 14:00)
messages.preview: Final banner set attached. Media needs your sign-off by 12:00 to hit the 2pm launch slot…
messages.body:
Morning Jordan,

The final **Northwind Outdoor** spring banners are attached: six sizes, with copy updated from the client's last round of comments.

Media needs your sign-off by **12:00** to traffic them for the 14:00 launch. If anything needs changing we have to know this morning; after lunch there's no time to re-export.

Thanks,
Tomás
messages.explanation: **Reply now.** A hard deadline *today*, with a team blocked on you. Approving final creative is the account manager's call, so it can't be delegated, and scheduling it for later risks missing the 12:00 cut-off. Check the six sizes against the client's comments and answer this morning; even "approved, go" is a two-minute job that unblocks three people.

messages.subject: PO number missing on invoice HSC-0412
messages.preview: We can't send the April invoice to Harbor Supply without their purchase order number…
messages.body:
Hi Jordan,

We can't issue invoice **HSC-0412** to Harbor Supply Co. until it carries their purchase order number. The draft is attached.

Could someone send us the PO by Wednesday so it goes out in this billing run?

Thanks,
Helen, Finance
messages.explanation: **Delegate.** Real, but not urgent and not yours to chase: your account coordinator keeps the PO log and can answer Finance in five minutes. Forward it with one line of context (*"Harbor Supply's April PO for Helen, please, by Wednesday"*). Replying yourself also gets it done, so it earns partial credit, but it spends your morning on admin someone else owns.

messages.subject: Can we move next Tuesday's review?
messages.preview: Our board meeting moved, so Tuesday at 11 no longer works. Could we do Wednesday or Thursday instead…
messages.body:
Hi Jordan,

Our board meeting has moved to next Tuesday morning, so our 11:00 performance review no longer works on my side. Could we do Wednesday or Thursday instead? Any time after 10 is fine.

No need for a new deck; the March numbers are what I want to go through.

Best,
Ben
messages.explanation: **Schedule.** A client request, but the meeting is a week away and Ben has offered flexible options. It needs a calendar decision, not an instant reply: check the team's availability after the all-hands and send a new invite today. Answering within the day keeps the relationship warm without pulling you away from this morning's urgent messages.

messages.subject: What's new in Pulse: custom dashboards and five more updates
messages.preview: This month: drag-and-drop widgets, scheduled exports and a refreshed date picker…
messages.body:
Hi there,

Here's what shipped in Pulse Analytics this month.

**Custom dashboards:** drag and drop widgets to build a view for each client.
**Scheduled exports:** send a PDF snapshot to your inbox every Monday.
**New date picker:** compare any two periods in two clicks.

Read the full release notes in your account.
messages.explanation: **Archive.** Useful someday, needed never at 9:00 on a Monday. A newsletter has no deadline and nobody waiting on you. Archive it (or filter these into a folder) so your inbox only holds things that need a decision. If a feature looks genuinely useful, the release notes will still be there on Friday.

messages.subject: Northwind March deck for Thursday's pitch?
messages.preview: We're pitching an outdoor gear brand on Thursday. Could I borrow the structure of your March Northwind deck…
messages.body:
Hey Jordan,

We're pitching an outdoor gear brand on **Thursday**, and your March Northwind performance deck is the best example we have of how we report. Could you send it over so we can reuse the structure?

No rush today; Wednesday is fine.

Aisha
messages.explanation: **Schedule.** Worth a yes, but nothing breaks before Wednesday, and the deck needs your judgement first: it is full of Northwind's confidential figures, which must come out before it is reused for another brand. Book 20 minutes this afternoon to strip the numbers and send it. Delegating to your coordinator works too *if* you spell out what to remove, so it earns partial credit.

content.summary: Triage is a judgement call, not a speed test. Fires first: the VIP client with a deadline and the creative team blocked on your approval. Report threats before anyone clicks. Then hand over what others own, book what can wait, and clear what needs nothing. Ten minutes of sorting at 9:00 protects the rest of your Monday.

modules.title: Escalate or handle?
modules.instructions: For each situation: **True** if you should escalate to your account director today.

statements.text: A client asks to move their launch by two days.
statements.explanation: A schedule change inside your remit. Confirm, update the plan, inform the team.

statements.text: A client says they are “reconsidering the relationship” in a status call.
statements.explanation: Any signal about the relationship itself goes up the same day.

statements.text: Spend is 40% over the monthly budget with ten days left.
statements.explanation: Money problems escalate immediately, with a fix proposed.

statements.text: A client asks for a report format we do not have yet.
statements.explanation: Agree a reasonable deadline and build it. Escalate only if it affects other accounts.
